title: Why Drying Potatoes Before Frying Is the Key to Preventing Oil Splatters
excerpt: Chef Ranveer Brar's go-to tip for safer, mess-free frying comes down to one overlooked step: removing surface moisture from cut potatoes before they hit the oil.
body:
• Moisture on potato surfaces is the primary cause of oil splatters during frying — water hitting hot oil instantly turns to steam, launching oil droplets out of the pan.
  • Thoroughly patting potatoes dry with a kitchen towel or paper towels before frying dramatically reduces splattering and improves crispiness.
  • Adding a pinch of salt to the oil before frying provides an additional layer of protection by absorbing residual moisture.
  • Soaking cut potatoes in water removes excess starch, but the drying step afterward is non-negotiable for safe frying.

Every Indian kitchen has a frying story gone wrong — the moment a freshly cut potato hits a kadai of hot oil and sends a cascade of scalding drops across the stovetop. Celebrity chef Ranveer Brar, known for his accessible cooking tips shared across social media, has a characteristically simple fix: dry your potatoes completely before they go anywhere near the oil.

The Science Behind the Splatter

Oil splatters are not caused by the oil itself but by water. When moisture on the surface of a potato makes contact with oil heated to 170–180°C, the water molecules rapidly convert to steam. That steam expands to roughly 1,700 times the volume of the original water, creating tiny explosions that launch oil droplets out of the pan.

"The real cause of those pesky splatters isn't the oil itself, but rather the steam created when the hot oil interacts with the food's evaporated water," explains a report from Mental Floss on the physics of frying. The wetter the ingredient, the more violent the reaction.

The Fix: Pat, Press, and Air-Dry

Brar's approach is rooted in the same principles taught in professional kitchens. After washing or soaking cut potatoes — a step most Indian cooks follow to remove excess starch — the critical move is thorough drying. Spread the potato pieces on a clean kitchen towel or a layer of paper towels, then pat them down firmly. For best results, let them air-dry for 10 to 15 minutes before frying.

This applies whether you are deep-frying for French fries, shallow-frying potato wedges, or making aloo bhajia in a kadai. The step works for all potato preparations and extends to other moisture-heavy vegetables like paneer, cauliflower florets, and raw banana slices that are commonly fried in Indian cooking.

The Salt Trick: An Extra Safeguard

A complementary technique, widely used by professional chefs including Sanjeev Kapoor, involves sprinkling a small pinch of salt into the oil before adding food. Salt absorbs residual surface moisture, reducing the water-oil reaction. According to food science experts, the salt doesn't eliminate splattering entirely but significantly dampens the effect.

The key is moderation — a pinch is sufficient. Adding too much salt before frying can over-season the food and draw out additional moisture from the potatoes, which defeats the purpose.

Why Indian Kitchens Are Especially Vulnerable

Indian cooking relies heavily on deep-frying — from samosas and pakoras to puris and aloo tikki. Unlike Western pan-frying with a thin layer of oil, kadai frying involves submerging food in several inches of hot oil, which amplifies the splatter risk. Indian households also typically wash and soak potatoes as a standard prep step, meaning the potatoes carry more surface moisture than in recipes that skip soaking.

"Before you fry, make sure to dry the potatoes thoroughly using paper towels or a clean kitchen towel. Excess moisture can cause oil splatters and prevent crispiness."

— Culinary experts at The Best of Culinary

The double-fry technique that Brar often uses in his French fries recipe — frying once at 130°C and again at 170°C — also reduces splattering during the second round, since much of the surface moisture has already been driven off during the initial fry.

Practical Tips for Safer Frying

Beyond drying, several other habits reduce splatter risk. Use a deep, round-bottomed kadai rather than a shallow pan — the taller walls contain errant oil drops. Never overcrowd the pan, as adding too many potatoes at once drops the oil temperature rapidly, causing aggressive bubbling. Place potatoes gently into the oil using a slotted spoon or tongs rather than dropping them from height.

For those who want to avoid frying splatter altogether, air fryers have become a popular alternative in Indian kitchens. Brar himself has shared air fryer recipes for potato wedges and falafel that achieve crispy results with minimal oil. But for those committed to the deep-fried crunch of a proper aloo bhajia or samosa, the drying step remains the single most effective safety measure.

The Takeaway

It is a small step that takes under a minute but can prevent burns, reduce kitchen cleanup, and — as a bonus — produce crispier fried potatoes. The next time you reach for the kadai, reach for the kitchen towel first.
